title: Chapter e9: Clinical Toxicology
source: DiPiro's Pharmacotherapy: A Pathophysiologic Approach, 13th Edition, Chapter e9 (Bryan D. Hayes; Natalija M. Farrell)
lecture: 10/13 and 10/14 (the updated syllabus lists 'Dipiro Chapter 9'); assigned in class on 10/14 for Treating Poisonings, which continues 10/19
about: The chapter provides an overview of foundational concepts of clinical toxicology: examples of the spectrum of toxicity, means to recognize poisoning risk, and principles of treatment. It covers the epidemiology of poisoning in the United States, poison prevention strategies such as child-resistant packaging, recognition and assessment of the poisoned patient including urine drug screening, and toxicokinetic considerations in overdose (Table e9-7). The General Approach to Treatment section covers prehospital first aid, hospital supportive care, gastric decontamination (ipecac syrup, single-dose activated charcoal, gastric lavage, whole-bowel irrigation), enhanced elimination and kidney replacement therapy, diuresis, multiple-dose activated charcoal, antidotes (Table e9-9) and how the effectiveness of therapies is assessed. The Clinical Spectrum of Poisoning section then presents acetaminophen, anticholinesterase insecticides, calcium channel antagonists, anticholinergics, opioids and weapons of mass chemical poisoning, each with clinical presentation, mechanism of toxicity, causative agents, incidence, risk assessment, management of toxicity, and monitoring and prevention. The chapter ends with key resources, guidelines, a bibliography and self-assessment questions with answers.

read_for: General Approach to Treatment - the section she told the class to read during the break and said she would use to generate discussion.
Perspectives on Gastric Decontamination: the AACT/EAPCCT position statements (clintox.org) that no gastric decontamination should be used routinely.

Single-Dose Activated Charcoal: the adult dose (25-100 g; 1 g/kg in children), effectiveness within 1 hour, the toxins it does not adsorb (iron, lead, lithium, alcohols, aliphatic hydrocarbons, corrosives), and the aspiration risk and contraindications.

Gastric Lavage: experienced clinicians only, life-threatening ingestions within 1 hour or substances not adsorbed by charcoal, intubation if no gag reflex, complications, and that fewer than 0.1% of cases received it in the 2022 APC-NPDS report.

Whole-Bowel Irrigation: GoLYTELY/Colyte for sustained-release or enteric-coated drugs, iron, lithium, potassium and swallowed drug packets; contraindications (ileus, obstruction, perforation, hemorrhage, unprotected airway).

Multiple-Dose Activated Charcoal: charcoal intestinal dialysis, interruption of enterohepatic recirculation, the five drugs for which it is recommended (carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine, theophylline), the 12.5-25 g every 2-6 h schedule and avoidance of sorbitol formulations.
Table e9-8 First Aid for Poison Exposures and Historical Prehospital Home Care: why ipecac syrup is no longer recommended or sold.
Toxicokinetic Considerations and Table e9-7: saturation of first-pass metabolism, concretions and slowed GI motility, decreased protein binding and saturated biotransformation in overdose.

Enhanced Elimination and Kidney Replacement Therapy: the physicochemical criteria for a dialyzable drug (Vd <1 L/kg, protein binding <80%, molecular weight <1,000 daltons) and the EXTRIP guidelines - she said she would talk about it.
Assessing Effectiveness of Therapies: why the evidence base is case reports, volunteer studies and in vitro adsorption tests rather than controlled trials.

terms.chapter_definition: Poisoning can result from exposure to excessive doses of any chemical, with medicines being responsible for most childhood and adult poisonings; virtually any chemical can become a poison when taken in enough quantity.

Compounds that produce characteristic clinical pictures (toxidromes), such as opioid poisoning with pinpoint pupils, central nervous system (CNS) depression, and respiratory depression, are most readily recognizable.

The pharmacokinetic characteristics of drugs taken in overdose may differ from those observed following therapeutic doses; the differences are the result of dose-dependent changes in absorption, distribution, metabolism, or elimination, pharmacologic effects of the drug, or pathophysiologic consequences of the overdose.

Induced vomiting with ipecac syrup was once routinely used to treat ingested poisons at home; in 2003 the American Academy of Pediatrics issued a policy statement that it should no longer be used routinely, and it is no longer manufactured in the United States.

a nontoxic, relatively inexpensive, purified form of carbon with a highly adsorbent surface that binds (adsorbs) a toxin in the GI tract; a slurry of activated charcoal in water is administered orally or via nasogastric tube.

washing out of gastric contents through an orogastric tube; if performed at all, should only be done by clinicians experienced in the procedure, and may be considered for potentially life-threatening ingestions when the ingestion occurred within 1 hour or when the substance is not adsorbed by activated charcoal.

Polyethylene glycol electrolyte solutions, such as GoLYTELY and Colyte, used routinely for whole-bowel irrigation prior to colonoscopy, administered orally or by nasogastric tube to decontaminate the GI tract of certain ingested substances.

the attraction of drug molecules across the capillary bed of the intestine by activated charcoal in the intestinal lumen and subsequent adsorption of the drug to the charcoal; multiple doses of activated charcoal can augment the body's clearance of certain drugs.
multiple-dose activated charcoal may interrupt the enterohepatic recirculation of certain drugs; once the drug is adsorbed to the charcoal, it is eliminated with the charcoal in the stool.

drugs with a small volume of distribution (<1 L/kg), low protein binding (<80%) and low molecular weight (<1,000 daltons) are generally considered dialyzable; hemodialysis is used in select situations such as methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylate and theophylline poisoning.
altering urinary pH may increase excretion of certain chemicals that are weak acids or bases by trapping ionized drug in the renal tubule and minimizing reabsorption.

Antidotes can prevent or reduce the toxicity of certain poisons, but symptomatic and supportive care is essential for all patients; specific systemic antidotes are available for some common poisonings (Table e9-9).

listen: This reading is Chapter e nine, Clinical Toxicology, by Bryan Hayes and Natalija Farrell, in DiPiro's Pharmacotherapy, A Pathophysiologic Approach, thirteenth edition. She called it the pharmacotherapy textbook and said she pulls chapters from it for her topics. She had the class read its General Approach to Treatment section, down to multiple dose activated charcoal, to see how the use of methods to prevent absorption has changed. Its later section on specific poisonings helps with her poisoning table. Overdose does change a drug's kinetics, most often its volume of distribution and its clearance. First pass metabolism saturates, so bioavailability rises. Only drugs with a small volume of distribution, low protein binding and low molecular weight are dialyzable, so a drug with a large volume of distribution is hard to remove by hemodialysis. The chapter states that emesis is no longer used, so it is not first line for an ingested poison. Ipecac syrup, once kept in homes, is no longer sold in the United States. The biggest risk of emesis is aspiration. Gastric lavage pumps fluid into the stomach through a tube and back out, only by experienced clinicians, and not with an esophageal rupture or stomach injury. Whole bowel irrigation uses a polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution such as GoLYTELY, and not with an ileus or a blockage in the gut. The American and European clinical toxicology groups state that no gastric decontamination method should be used routinely. She said they all call these methods dangerous and risky, to use only if you really think you have to, though experienced toxicologists may try them for a massive ingestion. Based on patient outcomes, she called charcoal probably your best option. It is a slurry in water, unpleasant and messy, and it can be aspirated. It does not bind everything. The chapter names iron, lead, lithium, alcohols, aliphatic hydrocarbons and corrosives. Her key says single dose charcoal is most likely to work less than sixty minutes after ingestion. In class she said up to two hours, and that they used to say just an hour. The limit exists because the poison moves on through, so charcoal must reach the stomach and small intestine while the poison is still there. Multiple dose activated charcoal is for a drug that undergoes enterohepatic recirculation. Each later dose catches drug the bile returns to the small intestine, and it leaves with the charcoal in the stool. Her table key cites DiPiro's Pharmacotherapy for two rows. Organophosphate insecticides cause acetylcholine excess, summed up as sludge or dumbbells. Atropine is a muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist. Pralidoxime removes the organophosphate from acetylcholinesterase. Iron causes vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea within one to six hours. Lethargy, coma, seizures, bloody vomiting, bloody diarrhea and shock, with hypotension and tachycardia, come within six to twenty four hours. Liver dysfunction and failure are possible in two to five days. Deferoxamine chelates the circulating ferric iron. The traps. Single dose charcoal binds poison still in the gut, and multiple dose charcoal catches a drug that recirculates through the bile. Charcoal does not bind iron, and the iron antidote is deferoxamine. Atropine blocks the muscarinic receptor, while pralidoxime frees acetylcholinesterase. The chapter's opioid toxidrome has pinpoint pupils, so larger pupils are not part of it.
